Intent for battery includes knowing with substantial certainty that contact will result.
Vosburg v. Putney
A wrongful kick in class was a battery, with liability for unforeseen severe consequences.
Fisher v. Carrousel Motor Hotel
Snatching a plate from a diner’s hand was an offensive contact with his person.
I de S et Ux v. W de S
Swinging a hatchet at a woman in the dark was an assault though no contact occurred.
Tuberville v. Savage
Words accompanying a gesture showed no immediate threat, so there was no assault.
Picard v. Barry Pontiac
Touching a camera the plaintiff was holding was an offensive contact.
White v. Muniz
Battery required intent that the contact be harmful or offensive.
Polmatier v. Russ
An insane person who formed intent to act could be liable for battery.
Bird v. Jones
Blocking a person’s path in one direction was not false imprisonment.
State Rubbish Collectors v. Siliznoff
Emotional distress caused by outrageous threats is actionable without physical injury.
Harris v. Jones
Mocking an employee’s stutter failed for lack of severe emotional distress.
Intel v. Hamidi
Unwanted emails that did not impair computer systems were not trespass to chattels.
Moore v. Regents
No conversion claim existed for a patient’s excised cells used in research.
Dougherty v. Stepp
Entering land without consent is actionable even without damage.
Herrin v. Sutherland
Firing shotguns through the airspace over land was a trespass.
Wishnatsky v. Huey
Briefly pushing a door on an intruder was not offensive to a reasonable person.
mcq: Dana pulls a chair away as Paul sits down. She meant only to startle him, not hurt him. Paul hits the floor. Is Dana liable for battery?
Yes: she was substantially certain he would hit the ground
No: she intended only to startle him, not to cause any harm
No: she never touched Paul herself
Only if Paul’s injury was serious
Garratt v. Dailey: intent means purpose or substantial certainty that the contact will occur. No intent to harm is required, and contact through the ground counts.
Which element is required for assault?
Apprehension of an imminent harmful or offensive contact
Actual physical contact with the plaintiff
Fear of a harmful contact at some later, unspecified time
Words threatening violence next week
Assault protects against apprehension (not fear) of imminent contact. Future threats and, usually, words alone are not enough.
Dev throws a rock at Ana, misses, and hits Ben. Can Ben sue Dev for battery?
Yes: his intent transfers to Ben
No: he had no intent toward Ben
Only in negligence, not battery
Only if Ben saw the rock coming
Transferred intent: intent toward one person carries over to the person actually harmed.
Hal builds a fence a few feet onto his neighbor's lot, honestly and reasonably believing the strip is his. Trespass to land?
Yes: intent to enter is enough; mistake is no defense
No: his honest and reasonable mistake about the line is a defense
No: the neighbor suffered no harm
Only if he had been warned first
Trespass requires only intent to enter the land. A good-faith mistake about ownership does not excuse it.
Rae takes her neighbor's car without permission, drives it across the country, and wrecks it. Most likely claim?
Conversion, because the interference was serious
Trespass to chattels, since she meant to give it back
No tort, since she meant to return it
Battery, because the car was damaged
Conversion is a serious interference justifying a forced sale at full value. A brief, harmless use would be trespass to chattels at most.
Ellie is shut in a room. A second door is unlocked, obvious, and safe to use. False imprisonment?
No: she knew of a reasonable way out
Yes: any confinement counts, whatever exits exist
Yes, if she felt humiliated
No: nobody touched her
Confinement must be complete. A reasonable, known means of escape defeats the claim.
A hotel manager snatches a plate from a diner's hand while shouting a slur, never touching his body. Battery?
Yes: touching something closely tied to the body counts
No: his body was never touched
No: words and gestures alone can never be a battery
Only if the diner was injured
Fisher v. Carrousel Motor Hotel: snatching an object from someone's hand is an offensive contact with the person.
D brutally beats Ann in front of her teenage son, knowing he is there. Can the son sue D for IIED?
Yes: he is immediate family and was present
No: the conduct wasn’t aimed at him
No: only the direct victim can recover
Only if he was physically hurt too
Restatement § 46(2): when conduct is directed at a third person, immediate family members present at the time may recover.
With his hand on his sword, a man says: 'If it were not assize-time, I would not take such language from you.' Assault?
No: his words negated any threat of imminent contact
Yes: putting his hand on the sword is itself a threat
Yes: any threat with a weapon is assault
Only if the listener was afraid
Tuberville v. Savage: words can strip a gesture of its menace.
In White v. Muniz, a woman with Alzheimer's struck her caregiver. The Colorado court required proof that she:
Intent to contact and intent that it harm or offend
Intent to make the contact, without any intent to harm or offend
Mere carelessness in making contact
Awareness that the contact was illegal
White applied the dual intent rule. Many courts use single intent: intent to contact is enough if the contact is in fact harmful or offensive.
In Polmatier v. Russ, a man in a psychotic state shot his father-in-law. Could he be liable for battery?
Yes: an insane person can form the needed intent
No: insanity is a complete defense to intentional torts
No: he couldn’t understand his acts
Only under a negligence theory
Insane people can be liable for intentional torts if they formed the intent to act, even from delusional reasons.
A mechanic, angry at being photographed, pokes the customer's camera without touching her. Picard v. Barry Pontiac result?
Battery, since the camera was closely tied to her
No tort, since only the camera and not her body was touched
Assault, but not battery
Trespass to chattels, but not battery
Contact with something closely attached to the plaintiff, like a camera she was holding, is contact with her.
Intel v. Hamidi: a former employee sent mass emails to Intel's servers, which kept working fine. Trespass to chattels?
No: the system itself wasn’t harmed
Yes: any unwanted use is trespass
Yes: employees were distracted
No trespass, but conversion instead
California requires actual impairment of the chattel for trespass to chattels. Lost productivity from content did not count.
Moore v. Regents: doctors used a patient's removed cells to develop a lucrative cell line. Could he sue for conversion?
No: the court wouldn’t extend conversion to his cells
Yes: his cells were his property
Yes, for the full value of the cell line developed
Only for trespass to chattels
The court rejected conversion but allowed a breach of fiduciary duty / informed consent claim.
Bird v. Jones: a crowd blocks a man's way on a bridge, but he can turn back and go another way. False imprisonment?
No: blocking one direction isn’t confinement
Yes: any obstruction of his chosen path confines him
Yes, if he was delayed
Only if police were involved
Confinement means being held within boundaries on all sides, not merely prevented from going one way.
Harris v. Jones: a supervisor repeatedly mocked an employee's stutter, and he was humiliated. The IIED claim failed because:
His distress wasn’t shown to be severe enough
Mocking a disability can never be outrageous conduct
There was no physical contact
The employer was immune
The court found the conduct outrageous, but the plaintiff did not prove severe emotional distress.
Rob walks across his neighbor's lawn without permission, causing no damage. The neighbor sues. Result?
Liable for at least nominal damages
Not liable without some damage
Liable only if he had been warned
Not liable, since lawns are open land
Dougherty v. Stepp: entering land without consent is actionable even without harm.
Herrin v. Sutherland: a hunter fired shots over the plaintiff's land without touching the ground. Trespass?
Yes: the shots invaded the airspace
No: nothing physically touched the ground
No: hunting is privileged
Only if livestock were hurt
Intrusions into the immediate airspace above land can be trespass. Modern law limits this to the zone of actual use.
A nurse kisses a sleeping patient, who never learns of it until later. Battery?
Yes: awareness at the time isn’t required
No: the patient didn’t know it happened
No: the patient wasn’t harmed
Only assault, since there was no fear
Offensive contact is battery even if the victim is asleep. Assault, by contrast, requires apprehension and thus awareness.
Wishnatsky v. Huey: an assistant attorney general briefly pushed a door shut on a man entering his office. Battery?
No: it wouldn’t offend a reasonable sense of dignity
Yes: any unwanted contact, however slight, is battery
Yes: he touched the man through the door
Only if the man fell
Offensiveness is judged objectively. A hypersensitive plaintiff cannot make ordinary contact offensive.
Which tort protects the right to exclusive possession of personal property, for minor interference that causes damage?
Trespass to chattels
Conversion
Trespass to land
Private nuisance
Trespass to chattels covers lesser interference with actual harm. Serious interference is conversion.
fill: Battery requires an intended harmful or ___ contact with the plaintiff’s person.
Assault requires reasonable apprehension of an ___ contact.
Words of future threat aren’t enough.
When a defendant intends to hit one person but hits another, intent is said to ___.
False imprisonment isn’t committed if there’s a known, reasonable means of ___.
Bird v. Jones and related rules.

topics.name: Tort Defenses & Immunities
terms: Consent
Willingness in fact for conduct to occur, shown by words or conduct.
Implied consent
Consent inferred from conduct, custom or circumstances.
Emergency exception
Consent implied for urgent treatment when a patient cannot consent and delay risks serious harm.
Self-defense
Privilege to use reasonable force one reasonably believes necessary to prevent imminent harmful contact.
Defense of others
Privilege to use reasonable force to protect a third person from attack.
Defense of property
Privilege to use reasonable, non-deadly force to prevent or end an intrusion on one’s land or chattels.
Recapture of chattels
Privilege to use reasonable force in fresh pursuit to regain wrongfully taken property.
Shopkeeper’s privilege
A merchant’s right to detain a suspected shoplifter reasonably, briefly and on reasonable belief.
Public necessity
Complete privilege to damage property to avert an imminent disaster to the community.
Private necessity
Incomplete privilege to use another’s property to prevent greater harm to oneself, paying for damage.
Contributory negligence
A plaintiff’s own carelessness, which at common law completely barred recovery.
Last clear chance
Doctrine letting a negligent plaintiff recover if the defendant had the final opportunity to avoid harm.
Pure comparative fault
Recovery reduced by the plaintiff’s percentage of fault, however large.
Modified comparative fault
Reduced recovery allowed only if the plaintiff’s fault stays below a 50% or 51% threshold.
Express assumption of risk
An explicit agreement, like a signed waiver, releasing the defendant from liability.
Primary assumption of risk
A no-duty rule for risks inherent in an activity the plaintiff chose.
Secondary assumption of risk
Knowingly encountering a risk created by the defendant’s negligence, now usually part of comparative fault.
Exculpatory clause
A contract term releasing a party from liability for its own negligence.
Statute of limitations
A deadline for filing suit, measured from when the claim accrues.
Discovery rule
Starts the limitations clock when the plaintiff knew or should have known of the injury and its cause.
Statute of repose
A fixed filing deadline measured from an event, such as a product’s sale, regardless of injury.
Sovereign immunity
Government immunity from suit unless it consents.
Federal Tort Claims Act
Federal statute waiving U.S. immunity for many negligence claims, with exceptions.
Discretionary function exception
FTCA bar on claims based on government policy judgments.
Feres doctrine
Bar on FTCA claims by service members for injuries incident to military service.
Charitable immunity
A former rule shielding charities from tort liability, now largely abolished.
Intrafamily immunity
A former bar on suits between spouses or between parents and children.
cases: Mohr v. Williams
Operating on a different ear than the one consented to was a battery.
O’Brien v. Cunard
Holding up an arm in a vaccination line manifested consent.
Hudson v. Craft
Consent to an illegal prize fight did not bar a fighter the statute protected.
Katko v. Briney
A spring gun protecting an empty farmhouse was unprivileged deadly force.
Courvoisier v. Raymond
Self-defense covers reasonable but mistaken belief in a threat.
Vincent v. Lake Erie
A ship kept moored in a storm under private necessity had to pay for dock damage.
Ploof v. Putnam
A dock owner could not unmoor a boat seeking shelter from a storm under necessity.
Surocco v. Geary
Destroying a house to stop a citywide fire was privileged public necessity.
Coblyn v. Kennedy’s
Detaining an elderly shopper without reasonable grounds exceeded the shopkeeper’s privilege.
Butterfield v. Forrester
A plaintiff’s own lack of ordinary care barred recovery.
Li v. Yellow Cab
California replaced contributory negligence with pure comparative fault.
Murphy v. Steeplechase Amusement
A rider accepted the obvious risks of a ride designed to make people fall.
Tunkl v. Regents
A hospital’s release of negligence liability violated public policy.
Knight v. Jewett
Sports coparticipants owe no duty to avoid ordinary carelessness inherent in the game.
mcq: A store detains a suspected shoplifter for 20 minutes, reasonably and on a reasonable belief. She turns out to be innocent. Is the store liable for false imprisonment?
No: the shopkeeper's privilege applies
Yes: liability is strict once she is innocent
Yes: any detention without a warrant is unlawful
No: there was no physical barrier
The shopkeeper's privilege covers a detention on reasonable belief, in a reasonable manner, for a reasonable time.
During a storm a ship stays moored to a dock and damages it (Vincent v. Lake Erie). Is the shipowner liable?
Yes: private necessity still requires paying for damage
No: necessity is a complete defense, so it owes nothing
No: storm damage is an act of God
Yes, including punitive damages
Private necessity lets the ship stay moored, but the owner must still pay for the damage it causes.
A patient consents to surgery on her right ear. The surgeon operates on the left ear instead, with no emergency. Battery?
Yes: the surgeon went beyond the consent given
No: the surgery was beneficial
No: consent to surgery covers related procedures
Only if the operation failed
Mohr v. Williams: acting outside the scope of consent is a battery even if skillful and in good faith.
Officials destroy a house to stop a fire from spreading across the city. Can the owner recover from them in tort?
No: public necessity is a complete privilege
Yes: private necessity requires payment
Yes: destruction of property is always compensable
Only if the fire never reached the house
Surocco v. Geary: public necessity is complete. Any compensation comes from statute or takings law.
Under traditional contributory negligence, a plaintiff who is 5% at fault recovers:
Nothing, unless last clear chance applies
95% of damages, reduced by her share
50% of damages, as a split
Full damages, since the defendant was worse
Contributory negligence was a complete bar, softened by last clear chance.
A plaintiff is 60% at fault and has $100,000 in damages. Under pure comparative negligence she recovers:
Pure comparative fault reduces recovery by the plaintiff's share. Under a modified 50% or 51% bar she would get nothing.
A plaintiff is 40% at fault with $100,000 in damages, in a modified comparative fault state with a 50% bar. She recovers:
Below the threshold, recovery is reduced by her share. At or above it (depending on the state's version), she recovers nothing.
A fan at a baseball game is hit by a foul ball in the stands. Typical result?
No recovery: primary assumption of an inherent risk
Full recovery: the stadium is strictly liable
Recovery reduced by comparative fault
Recovery only if she sat in the bleachers
Primary assumption of risk means no duty to protect against risks inherent in the activity.
A hospital requires every patient to sign a release of all negligence claims before treatment. Is it enforceable?
No: releases for essential public services are void
Yes: the patient signed it voluntarily and knowingly
Yes, if the release was printed in bold
Only for minor injuries during treatment
Tunkl v. Regents: exculpatory clauses are unenforceable where the service is essential and bargaining power unequal.
O'Brien v. Cunard: a passenger held up her arm in a line of people receiving vaccinations. Consent?
Yes: her conduct showed consent
No: consent must be given in words, not gestures
No: she was under duress
Only if she signed a form
Consent can be implied from conduct. The surgeon reasonably relied on her apparent willingness.
Courvoisier v. Raymond: a shopkeeper shot a man he reasonably but mistakenly believed was attacking him. Privilege?
Yes: self-defense covers reasonable mistakes
No: the man was innocent, so he’s liable
No: deadly force is never privileged
Only if the man was armed
Self-defense turns on what the defendant reasonably believed, not on the actual facts.
A homeowner sees a trespasser walking across her lawn. Before using any force to remove him, she generally must:
Ask him to leave, unless that’s futile or dangerous
Call the police before doing anything
Post a sign warning him to stay off
Nothing; reasonable force is always allowed right away
Defense of property requires a request to leave first unless it would be useless, and force must be reasonable and non-deadly.
Knight v. Jewett: a woman was hurt in a casual touch football game. Coparticipants in sports are liable only for:
Intentional injury or reckless conduct
Any careless play during the game
All contact, since football is risky
Nothing at all
Primary assumption of risk: no duty to avoid ordinary carelessness inherent in the sport.
Li v. Yellow Cab is known for:
Adopting pure comparative negligence in California
Creating the attractive nuisance doctrine
Abolishing strict products liability
Recognizing the tort of IIED
California replaced contributory negligence with pure comparative fault.
Murphy v. Steeplechase Amusement: a man was hurt on 'The Flopper,' a ride designed to make people fall. Cardozo held:
No recovery: he accepted an obvious risk
The park was strictly liable
Comparative fault split the loss
The ride was an attractive nuisance
Volunteers accept the obvious, inherent dangers of a sport or amusement.
Under the Federal Tort Claims Act, a claim attacking an agency's policy decision about how to allocate safety funding is barred by the:
Discretionary function exception
Feres doctrine
Statute of repose
Firefighter's rule
The FTCA waives immunity for ordinary negligence but bars claims based on policy judgments.
A surgeon leaves a sponge in a patient, who discovers it seven years later. The limitations period is two years. In most states:
The discovery rule starts the clock when she knew or should have known
The claim is barred, since seven years have passed since surgery
There is no limitations period for medical claims
She must sue within 30 days of discovery
The discovery rule delays accrual until the plaintiff knew or reasonably should have known of the injury and its cause.
Under the Feres doctrine, a service member injured by military doctors' negligence during service generally:
Cannot sue the United States under the FTCA
Can sue like any civilian
Can sue the military doctors personally for malpractice
Gets punitive damages
Feres bars FTCA claims for injuries incident to military service.
Charitable and intrafamily immunities today are best described as:
Largely abolished or narrowed
Expanding in most states
Absolute in most states
Limited to intentional torts
Most states have eliminated charitable immunity and narrowed parent-child and spousal immunity.
fill: Private necessity is an ___ privilege, so the actor must pay for damage caused.
Self-defense allows force that is ___ to the threat reasonably perceived.
In pure comparative fault states, a plaintiff’s recovery is reduced by her percentage of ___.
At common law, a plaintiff’s contributory negligence was a ___ bar to recovery.

topics.name: Negligence & Duty
terms: Negligence
Failure to use the care a reasonable person would use under the circumstances.
Duty
A legal obligation to conform to a standard of conduct to protect others from unreasonable risk.
Breach
Failure to meet the applicable standard of care.
Reasonable person
The objective standard of an ordinarily prudent person in the same circumstances.
Hand formula
Negligence when the burden of precaution is less than the probability of harm times its gravity.
Negligence per se
Using a statute’s requirement as the standard of care when the plaintiff and harm fall within its purpose.
Res ipsa loquitur
An inference of negligence when an accident ordinarily would not happen without negligence by the party in control.
Custom
Industry practice, which is evidence of the standard of care but usually not conclusive.
Malpractice
Professional negligence, measured by the customary practice of the profession.
Informed consent
A doctor’s duty to disclose material risks a reasonable patient would want to know.
Invitee
An entrant on business or public invitation, owed reasonable care including inspection.
Licensee
A social guest or entrant with permission, owed a warning of known concealed dangers.
Trespasser (land entrant)
Someone on land without permission, generally owed only freedom from willful or wanton harm.
Attractive nuisance
A duty to child trespassers for artificial conditions likely to lure and injure them.
Misfeasance
Active conduct that creates a risk, generally triggering a duty of care.
Nonfeasance
A failure to act, which generally triggers no duty without a special relationship.
Special relationship
A connection, such as innkeeper and guest, that creates an affirmative duty to protect.
Good Samaritan statute
A law shielding voluntary rescuers from liability for ordinary negligence.
Negligent infliction of emotional distress
Liability for mental harm caused by carelessness, limited by tests like zone of danger.
Zone of danger
A test allowing emotional distress recovery to those at risk of physical impact.
Bystander recovery
Damages for a close relative who perceives a serious injury to a family member.
Respondeat superior
An employer’s liability for employees’ torts committed within the scope of employment.
Vicarious liability
Responsibility imposed on one person for another’s tort because of their relationship.
Independent contractor
A hired party not controlled by the hirer, whose torts usually do not create vicarious liability.
Frolic
An employee’s substantial departure from work for personal purposes.
Detour
A minor deviation from work that stays within the scope of employment.
Nondelegable duty
A duty whose breach makes the hirer liable even if a contractor performed the work.
Negligent entrustment
Liability for supplying a dangerous item to someone known to be incompetent to use it.
Dram shop act
A statute making alcohol sellers liable for harm caused by intoxicated or underage customers.
Economic loss rule
A bar on negligence recovery for purely financial losses without physical harm.
Firefighter’s rule
A bar on public safety officers suing for the negligence that created the emergency.
cases: Brown v. Kendall
Unintentional injury requires proof of fault, not mere directness.
Vaughan v. Menlove
Negligence is judged by an objective reasonable person, not the defendant’s best judgment.
United States v. Carroll Towing
Negligence exists when the burden of precaution is less than probability times loss.
The T.J. Hooper
Following industry custom does not conclusively establish due care.
Martin v. Herzog
Unexcused violation of a safety statute is negligence in itself.
Tedla v. Ellman
Violating a safety statute was excused because compliance was more dangerous.
Gorris v. Scott
Negligence per se failed because the harm was not the type the statute addressed.
Byrne v. Boadle
A barrel falling from a warehouse window raised an inference of negligence.
Ybarra v. Spangard
Res ipsa applied against all medical staff in control of an unconscious patient.
Robinson v. Lindsay
A child driving a snowmobile was held to the adult standard of care.
Breunig v. American Family
Sudden mental illness excuses negligence only if it strikes without forewarning.
Roberts v. Ring
An elderly driver’s infirmities did not lower the standard of care.
Helling v. Carey
Failing to give a cheap glaucoma test was negligent despite medical custom.
Canterbury v. Spence
Doctors must disclose risks a reasonable patient would find material.
Rowland v. Christian
Land entrant categories gave way to a general duty of reasonable care.
Tarasoff v. Regents
A therapist must use reasonable care to protect a patient’s identifiable intended victim.
Kline v. 1500 Massachusetts Ave.
A landlord must take reasonable steps against foreseeable crime in common areas.
Yania v. Bigan
Taunting a man into danger and failing to rescue him created no liability.
H.R. Moch v. Rensselaer Water
A utility owed no duty to residents for failing to supply enough pressure to fight a fire.
Strauss v. Belle Realty
A utility owed no duty to a non-customer tenant injured during a blackout.
Thing v. La Chusa
Bystander recovery requires presence at the scene and awareness of the injury as it occurs.
Dillon v. Legg
A mother who saw her child killed could recover for emotional distress as a bystander.
Falzone v. Busch
A plaintiff in the zone of danger may recover for fright without impact.
Ira S. Bushey & Sons v. United States
An employer is liable for conduct characteristic of its enterprise, even a drunk sailor’s act.
mcq: Under the Hand formula, the precaution costs $100, the probability of accident is 1%, and the loss would be $50,000. Is failing to take the precaution negligent?
Yes: $100 is less than the expected loss of $500
No: the $100 burden exceeds the expected loss
No: a 1% risk is too small to matter
It depends only on industry custom
Carroll Towing: negligent if B is less than P × L. Here 0.01 × $50,000 = $500.
Under the Hand formula, a guardrail costs $2,000, the chance of an accident without it is 1%, and the expected loss is $100,000. Negligent to skip it?
No: B ($2,000) exceeds P × L ($1,000)
Yes: any feasible precaution is required
Yes: the loss is large
It depends on custom alone
P × L = $1,000, less than the $2,000 burden, so the formula says the omission was not negligent.
In Vaughan v. Menlove, the haystack owner argued he acted to the best of his own judgment. The court held:
An objective reasonable-person standard
An honest good-faith standard based on his own judgment
Each person’s own intelligence
A standard requiring intent
The standard is objective. A defendant's own poor judgment does not lower it.
A 14-year-old injures someone while driving a snowmobile. Which standard applies?
The adult standard, for an adult activity
The standard of a reasonable child his age
No duty, since minors can’t be negligent
Strict liability
Robinson v. Lindsay: children doing adult, dangerous activities get the adult standard.
A statute requires livestock on ships to be penned to prevent disease. Unpenned sheep wash overboard. Negligence per se?
No: the statute targeted disease, not drowning
Yes: any violation is negligence per se
Yes: the owner was in the protected class
No: statutes never set the standard
Gorris v. Scott: the harm must be of the type the statute targets.
Which is NOT required for res ipsa loquitur?
The plaintiff must identify the specific negligent act
The accident ordinarily does not happen without negligence
The instrumentality was in the defendant's control
The plaintiff did not contribute to the accident
Res ipsa exists because the plaintiff cannot pinpoint the specific act.
In The T.J. Hooper, tugboats lacked radios, as did most of the industry. Effect of following custom?
Evidence of care, but not conclusive
A complete defense, since they followed industry practice
Irrelevant to negligence
Conclusive proof of negligence
Courts, not industries, set the standard. Medical malpractice is the main exception.
Under the traditional categories, a social guest is hurt by a hidden hazard the host knew about. What duty did the host owe?
To warn of or fix known hidden dangers
To inspect for unknown dangers
Only to avoid willful or wanton harm
No duty at all
Social guests are licensees. Invitees are also owed reasonable inspection.
In a state following Thing v. La Chusa, a mother learns of her child's accident and arrives minutes later. Can she recover as a bystander for NIED?
No: she didn’t perceive the injury as it happened
Yes: she is a close relative
Yes: her emotional distress was entirely foreseeable
Only if she later had symptoms
Thing requires a close relationship, presence at the scene with awareness of the injury, and serious distress.
Breunig v. American Family: a driver had a sudden delusion and crashed. When can sudden mental illness excuse negligence?
When it strikes suddenly without warning
Never; mental illness is no excuse
Whenever the driver is mentally ill
Only if the driver is a minor
Breunig was liable because she had prior warning of her delusions.
Martin v. Herzog (Cardozo): a buggy drove at night without the lights a statute required. The unexcused violation was:
Negligence in itself
Merely evidence of negligence
Irrelevant
Strict liability
Unexcused violation of a safety statute is negligence per se, though causation must still be proved.
Helling v. Carey: ophthalmologists customarily did not test patients under 40 for glaucoma. The court held:
The test was required despite the custom
Custom set the medical standard of care
The plaintiff assumed the risk
No duty existed
Helling is an outlier applying a Hand-style analysis to override medical custom.
Canterbury v. Spence adopted which informed consent standard?
What a reasonable patient would consider material
What reasonable doctors customarily disclose
Whatever the doctor subjectively believes
No disclosure is required
Many states follow Canterbury's patient-centered standard, while others use the physician standard.
Yania v. Bigan: Bigan taunted Yania into jumping into a water-filled trench, then did nothing as he drowned. Liability?
No: he used no force and had no duty to rescue
Yes: he caused the peril
Yes: taunting creates a special relationship
Yes, as an intentional tort
Mere words and failure to rescue did not create liability, illustrating the no-duty-to-rescue rule.
Tarasoff v. Regents held that a therapist whose patient presents a serious danger of violence to an identifiable victim must:
Use reasonable care to protect the victim
Keep all communications confidential
Do nothing; there’s no duty to rescue
Notify the patient’s family only
The special relationship with the patient grounded a duty to protect third parties.
Rowland v. Christian replaced the invitee/licensee/trespasser categories with:
A general duty of reasonable care
Strict liability for landowners
No duty to anyone on the land
Duties only to invitees
California adopted ordinary negligence for land entrants. Many states kept the categories.
H.R. Moch v. Rensselaer Water: a water company failed to supply enough pressure, and a building burned. Liability to the owner?
No: it owed no duty to the public under its city deal
Yes: it breached its agreement with the city, so residents can sue
Yes: water supply is abnormally dangerous
Yes: under res ipsa loquitur
Cardozo limited duty to avoid indefinite liability to the whole public.
Strauss v. Belle Realty: during a citywide blackout, a tenant fell on dark stairs in a common area. The utility:
Owed no duty to him there
Was strictly liable
Was liable under negligence per se
Owed a duty to every New Yorker
Courts limited duty to avoid crushing liability from a single event affecting millions.
Ira S. Bushey & Sons v. United States: a drunk sailor returning to his ship opened drydock valves. The government was liable because:
It was characteristic of the enterprise
The sailor was an independent contractor
He acted to serve his employer
Drydocks are abnormally dangerous
Judge Friendly used a foreseeability, enterprise-risk view of respondeat superior.
An employer is usually NOT vicariously liable for the negligence of:
An independent contractor
An employee acting within the scope of employment
An employee on a minor detour
A delivery driver on her route
Exceptions include nondelegable duties and inherently dangerous work.
A delivery driver goes two blocks off route to buy coffee and hits a pedestrian. Most likely:
A detour, so the employer is liable
A frolic, so the employer isn’t liable
The driver alone is immune
The pedestrian assumed the risk
Minor deviations are detours. A substantial personal departure would be a frolic.
Ann lends her car keys to her friend, whom she knows is very drunk. He crashes. Ann's own liability is best described as:
Negligent entrustment
Respondeat superior
Strict liability
No liability: she was not driving
Supplying a dangerous instrumentality to someone you know is incompetent is negligence.
At common law, are parents vicariously liable for their children's torts simply because they are parents?
No, but they may be liable for negligent supervision
Yes, parents are always vicariously liable for their kids
Only for their children’s intentional torts
Only if the child is over 16 years old
Many states have limited statutes, but status alone does not create common-law vicarious liability.
A shopper in a supermarket is a classic example of a(n):
Invitee
Licensee
Trespasser
Social guest
Business visitors are invitees, owed reasonable care including inspection for hazards.
Which is NOT a typical element of the attractive nuisance doctrine?
The child was invited onto the land
The owner knows children are likely to trespass
The condition poses an unreasonable risk to children
Children do not appreciate the danger
The doctrine protects child trespassers, so invitation is not required.
A firefighter is injured fighting a fire the homeowner negligently started. Under the traditional firefighter's rule:
The firefighter can’t recover for that negligence
The firefighter recovers in full from the owner
The homeowner is strictly liable for the fire
Only the city can sue for the injury
The rule bars public safety officers from suing for the negligence that created the emergency.
Falzone v. Busch: a car nearly hit a woman, who became ill from fright. Under the zone of danger rule she:
May recover, since she was at risk of impact
May not recover without impact
May recover only if a relative was hurt
May recover only for property damage
Falzone dropped the impact requirement for plaintiffs in the zone of danger.
Dillon v. Legg allowed a mother's bystander recovery, considering whether she:
Was nearby, saw it, and was closely related
Was physically touched
Was in the zone of danger herself
Had a contract with the driver
Thing v. La Chusa later turned these factors into firm requirements.
Ybarra v. Spangard: a patient woke from an appendectomy with a shoulder injury. Res ipsa applied against:
Everyone who had control of him while unconscious
Only the surgeon who performed the operation
Nobody, since he couldn’t identify who caused it
The hospital alone, as the employer
The court shifted the burden to those in control to explain what happened.
fill: Under the Hand formula, negligence exists when the burden of precaution is less than P × ___.
Violating a safety statute may be negligence ___ if the plaintiff is in the protected class.
Res ipsa loquitur lets a jury infer negligence when the accident ordinarily doesn’t happen without ___.
Under respondeat superior, an employer is liable for torts committed within the scope of ___.

topics.name: Causation & Damages
terms: Cause in fact
Actual causation: the harm would not have occurred without the defendant’s conduct.
But-for test
Asks whether the harm would have happened without the defendant’s negligence.
Substantial factor test
A causation test for multiple causes, each sufficient alone to produce the harm.
Proximate cause
A legal limit on liability to harms within the scope of the risk that made the conduct negligent.
Foreseeability
Whether a reasonable person would anticipate the type of harm or plaintiff.
Intervening cause
A force that acts after the defendant’s conduct and contributes to the harm.
Superseding cause
An unforeseeable intervening cause that relieves the original defendant of liability.
Eggshell plaintiff rule
The defendant is liable for the full extent of injury even if the victim was unusually fragile.
Alternative liability
Burden-shifting when several negligent defendants exist and one caused the harm.
Market share liability
Apportioning responsibility among makers of a fungible product by their portion of sales.
Loss of chance
Recovery for a reduced likelihood of survival or a better outcome caused by negligence.
Joint and several liability
Each liable defendant can be made to pay the plaintiff’s entire damages.
Several liability
Each defendant pays only its proportionate share of damages.
Contribution
Recovery by a defendant who paid more than its share from the other liable defendants.
Indemnity
Shifting the entire loss from one defendant to another.
Compensatory damages
Money to restore the plaintiff to her position before the injury.
Punitive damages
Damages to punish and deter malicious, willful or reckless misconduct.
Nominal damages
A small sum awarded when a right was violated without actual loss.
Collateral source rule
Bars reducing damages for benefits the plaintiff received from independent payers like insurers.
Wrongful death action
A statutory claim by survivors for their own losses when someone is killed.
Survival action
A claim preserving the decedent’s own causes of action for the estate.
Avoidable consequences
A rule barring recovery for harm the plaintiff could have avoided with reasonable care after injury.
Remittitur
A court’s reduction of an excessive jury award as an alternative to a new trial.
Loss of consortium
A spouse’s or family member’s claim for lost companionship caused by injury to the victim.
cases: Palsgraf v. Long Island R.R.
No duty is owed to a plaintiff outside the foreseeable zone of danger.
In re Polemis
A negligent defendant is liable for all direct consequences, foreseeable or not.
Wagon Mound No. 1
Liability is limited to harm of a reasonably foreseeable type.
Kingston v. Chicago & N.W. Ry.
Each negligent fire combining to destroy property is a cause.
New York Central v. Grimstad
Without proof a life buoy would have saved the victim, causation failed.
Summers v. Tice
When two negligent hunters fired and one hit, each had to prove he was not the cause.
Sindell v. Abbott Laboratories
DES makers could be held liable by their share of the market.
Hymowitz v. Eli Lilly
National market share liability applied with no exculpation for proving non-supply.
Zuchowicz v. United States
Causation may be inferred when negligence increases the risk of the harm that occurs.
Herskovits v. Group Health
A negligently reduced chance of survival is itself a compensable harm.
Benn v. Thomas
A defendant takes a victim with a weak heart as he finds him.
Wagner v. International Railway
Danger invites rescue, so rescuers can recover from the negligent party.
Derdiarian v. Felix Contracting
A foreseeable intervening driver did not cut off a contractor’s liability.
Watson v. Kentucky & Indiana Bridge
A malicious intervening act could supersede the original negligence.
Ryan v. New York Central
A railroad’s fire liability was limited to the first house burned.
BMW of North America v. Gore
Punitive damages are reviewed for reprehensibility, ratio and comparable penalties.
State Farm v. Campbell
Punitive ratios beyond single digits rarely satisfy due process.
Stubbs v. City of Rochester
A plaintiff need not exclude every other cause to prove causation.
mcq: Palsgraf (Cardozo): a guard's push causes fireworks to explode, and scales fall on Mrs. Palsgraf far away. Why no liability?
No duty was owed to her: she was not a foreseeable plaintiff
The guard was not negligent at all in pushing the passenger
Her own negligence barred recovery
The fireworks owner was the only defendant
Cardozo: duty runs only to plaintiffs within the foreseeable zone of danger.
Which view says everyone owes a duty to the world at large, with proximate cause limited by policy and 'practical politics'?
Judge Andrews's Palsgraf dissent
Cardozo’s Palsgraf majority opinion
Wagon Mound No. 1
Summers v. Tice
Andrews treats the question as proximate cause, a policy limit.
Two independent fires, each enough on its own to burn the plaintiff's house, merge and destroy it. Causation test?
Substantial factor: each fire is a cause
But-for: neither defendant is liable
Only the first fire's starter is liable
Res ipsa loquitur
With multiple sufficient causes the but-for test fails, so courts use substantial factor (Kingston; Anderson).
Two hunters negligently fire toward the plaintiff. One pellet hits him, but no one can tell whose. Summers v. Tice result?
Each defendant must prove he didn’t cause it
The plaintiff loses for failing to prove which one did it
Each pays half no matter what
Only the better shot is liable
Alternative liability: each must exculpate himself or be jointly liable.
Defendant negligently taps the plaintiff, who has an unusually thin skull and suffers severe injury. Damages?
Full damages for the actual injury
Only what an ordinary person would suffer
None, since the injury was unforeseeable
Only nominal damages
The eggshell plaintiff rule: once some injury is foreseeable, the defendant bears its full extent.
Wagon Mound No. 1 replaced the Polemis rule with which test?
Liability only for foreseeable kinds of harm
Liability for all direct consequences of negligence
Strict liability for oil spills
The Hand formula
Proximate cause turns on foreseeability of the kind of harm.
A passenger is thrown from a negligently run train. His cousin goes to look for him and falls. Can the cousin recover?
Yes: danger invites rescue
No: the cousin assumed the risk
No: he was outside the zone of danger
Only if he was a professional rescuer
Wagner v. International Railway (Cardozo): rescuers are foreseeable plaintiffs.
D leaves an unguarded trench in a street. Another driver's foreseeable negligence pushes P into it. Is D liable?
Yes: a foreseeable intervening act doesn’t cut it off
No: the other driver is the only cause
No: any intervening act breaks the causal chain
Only if D intended the harm
Only unforeseeable intervening acts, often intentional crimes, supersede the original negligence.
A plaintiff injured by DES her mother took cannot identify which manufacturer made the pills. Sindell v. Abbott Labs allowed:
Market-share liability
No recovery without identification
Liability for the largest maker only
Recovery from the pharmacy only
Sindell apportioned liability by market share among makers of the fungible drug.
Punitive damages in tort typically require:
Malice or reckless disregard for others
Ordinary negligence
Any physical injury
A contract between the parties
Ordinary negligence supports only compensatory damages.
In re Polemis: a plank dropped into a ship's hold caused a spark that burned the ship. The court held the defendant liable for:
All direct consequences, even unforeseeable ones
Only the harm that was reasonably foreseeable
Nothing, since the fire was unforeseeable
Half the damage, as a compromise
Polemis's directness test was later rejected by Wagon Mound No. 1.
New York Central v. Grimstad: a barge captain fell overboard and drowned; the boat had no life buoy. The claim failed because:
No proof a buoy would have saved him
The railroad owed no duty
He assumed the risk
No statute required buoys
The plaintiff could not show but-for causation.
Zuchowicz v. United States: a patient got a drug overdose and later a rare lung disease. Judge Calabresi held causation could be inferred because:
The act was known to raise the risk of that harm
Res ipsa loquitur applied
The government admitted causation at trial
Overdoses carry strict liability
When negligence raises the risk of exactly the harm that happens, a jury may infer causation.
Herskovits v. Group Health: negligent diagnosis reduced a patient's survival chance from 39% to 25%. The court allowed:
Recovery for the lost chance
No recovery, since survival was under 50%
Full wrongful death damages
Only punitive damages
Loss-of-chance doctrine values the reduced chance itself.
Benn v. Thomas: a car accident bruised a man with a heart condition, and he died of a heart attack days later. The rule applied was:
The eggshell plaintiff rule
Superseding cause
Contributory negligence
Assumption of risk
Pre-existing conditions don't cut off liability for the full harm.
Watson v. Kentucky & Indiana Bridge: gasoline leaked from a derailed car, and a man threw a match. If he did so maliciously:
His intentional act was a superseding cause
The railroad remained fully liable for the explosion
Liability was split evenly
No one was liable
Foreseeable negligent intervention doesn't supersede; a malicious act might.
Hymowitz v. Eli Lilly adopted a national market share approach in which a DES maker:
Could not escape by proving it didn't make the pills the mother took
Could escape liability by proving it didn’t make those pills
Was jointly liable for all damages
Paid only if it was the largest seller
Liability tracked each maker's share of the national risk it created.
BMW of North America v. Gore set guideposts for reviewing punitive damages. Which is one of them?
The punitive-to-compensatory ratio
The defendant’s net worth alone
The jury’s deliberation time
Whether the plaintiff hired an expert
The guideposts: reprehensibility, ratio to actual harm, and comparable civil penalties.
State Farm v. Campbell suggested that punitive-to-compensatory ratios of what size are most likely to satisfy due process?
Single digits
Any size
Less than 1
The Court indicated few awards exceeding a single-digit ratio will satisfy due process.
Under the traditional collateral source rule, if the plaintiff's health insurer paid her $20,000 in medical bills, the defendant pays:
The full $20,000 anyway
Nothing for those bills
Half the bills
Only if the insurer sues
The tortfeasor gets no credit for independent benefits. Many states have modified the rule by statute.
A decedent's claim for her own pain before death is brought in a:
Survival action
Wrongful death action
Loss of consortium claim
Contribution action
Wrongful death compensates the survivors' own losses; survival preserves the decedent's claims.
D1 pays a $100,000 judgment under joint and several liability, though D1 and D2 were equally at fault. D1 may seek:
Contribution of $50,000 from D2
Nothing from D2
Indemnity of $100,000 from the plaintiff
Punitive damages from D2
Contribution spreads the loss among jointly liable tortfeasors.
A plaintiff refuses a simple, safe surgery that would have cured her injury. Her damages for the lasting harm are:
Reduced for failing to mitigate
Unaffected by her refusal
Increased for her suffering
Barred entirely by her fault
The avoidable consequences doctrine limits recovery for harm reasonable care would have prevented.
Ryan v. New York Central (1866): a railroad's negligent fire spread to many houses. The court limited liability to:
The first house the fire reached
Every house that burned
Houses within one mile
Nothing at all
Ryan is an early, now-criticized limit on proximate cause.
Stubbs v. City of Rochester: a man got typhoid after the city negligently mixed drinking and sewer water. He proved causation by:
Reasonable certainty that the water caused it
Eliminating every other possible cause of the illness
Using res ipsa loquitur
Showing the city was strictly liable
The plaintiff need not exclude all other causes, only make his theory more probable.
fill: The ‘but-for’ test asks whether the harm would have occurred ___ the defendant’s conduct.
Under the eggshell plaintiff rule, the defendant takes the plaintiff as he ___ him.
Wagon Mound No. 1 limited liability to harm of a reasonably ___ type.
An unforeseeable intervening act that cuts off liability is a ___ cause.

topics.name: Strict & Products Liability
terms: Strict liability
Liability without proof of fault.
Abnormally dangerous activity
Conduct whose serious risks remain even with reasonable care and that is not common usage.
Common usage
A factor against strict liability when many people customarily carry on the activity.
Wild animal rule
Possessors of undomesticated creatures are strictly liable for harm from their dangerous propensities.
Scienter (animals)
Knowledge of a domestic animal’s dangerous propensity, which triggers strict liability.
Products liability
Liability of commercial sellers for injuries caused by defective products.
Manufacturing defect
A product that departs from its intended design.
Design defect
A design whose risks could have been reduced by a reasonable alternative design.
Warning defect
Inadequate instructions or cautions about foreseeable, non-obvious risks.
Consumer expectations test
A product is defective if more dangerous than an ordinary buyer would anticipate.
Risk-utility test
Weighs a design’s dangers against its benefits and feasible alternatives.
Reasonable alternative design
A safer, feasible design whose omission makes a product not reasonably safe.
Learned intermediary doctrine
A drug maker satisfies its warning duty by warning the prescribing doctor.
Privity
A direct contractual relationship between parties.
Product misuse
An unforeseeable use of a product that can bar or reduce recovery.
Implied warranty of merchantability
A contract-based promise that goods are fit for their ordinary purpose.
Federal preemption
Federal law displacing state tort claims.
Private nuisance
Substantial and unreasonable interference with another’s use and enjoyment of land.
Public nuisance
Unreasonable interference with a right common to the general community.
Coming to the nuisance
Moving near an existing nuisance, a factor but usually not a complete defense.
Rylands doctrine
Strict liability for escape of a dangerous thing brought onto land for a non-natural use.
Special injury rule
A private plaintiff suing for public nuisance must show harm different in kind from the public’s.
cases: Rylands v. Fletcher
A landowner whose reservoir escaped was liable without negligence.
Indiana Harbor Belt v. American Cyanamid
Shipping a toxic chemical was not abnormally dangerous, since care could prevent spills.
Spano v. Perini
Blasters are strictly liable for vibration damage without physical invasion.
Madsen v. East Jordan Irrigation
Strict liability did not cover mink killing their kits after blasting noise.
MacPherson v. Buick Motor Co.
A manufacturer owes a duty of care to users without privity.
Escola v. Coca-Cola Bottling
A concurrence argued manufacturers should be strictly liable for defective products.
Greenman v. Yuba Power Products
A manufacturer is strictly liable in tort for defective goods that cause injury.
Barker v. Lull Engineering
Design defect can be shown by consumer expectations or risk-benefit with a burden shift.
Soule v. General Motors
The consumer expectations test does not fit complex technical designs.
Hood v. Ryobi
Clear warnings were adequate without describing every possible consequence.
MacDonald v. Ortho Pharmaceutical
Oral contraceptive makers must warn patients directly.
Riegel v. Medtronic
State tort claims about devices with FDA premarket approval are preempted.
Wyeth v. Levine
State failure-to-warn claims about drug labels were not preempted.
Boomer v. Atlantic Cement
A nuisance was remedied with permanent damages instead of an injunction.
Spur Industries v. Del E. Webb
A feedlot was enjoined, but the developer who came to it had to pay relocation costs.
Fontainebleau Hotel v. Forty-Five Twenty-Five
There is no right to light and air from a neighbor’s land.
mcq: A contractor uses dynamite with every possible precaution and still damages a neighbor's house. Is the contractor liable?
Yes: blasting carries strict liability
No: he used due care
Only if a statute was violated
Only if the neighbor was a licensee
Abnormally dangerous activities carry strict liability because care cannot eliminate their risks.
A pet tiger escapes and mauls a neighbor despite a sturdy cage. A dog with no history of biting bites a neighbor. Which owner is strictly liable?
The tiger’s owner, unless the dog’s owner knew of danger
Both owners, under strict liability for animals
Neither owner, unless one of them was negligent
The dog’s owner only
Wild animal owners are strictly liable; domestic animal owners only with known dangerous propensity.
One soda bottle in a batch contains a glass shard; all the others are fine. What kind of defect?
Manufacturing defect
Design defect
Warning defect
No defect: one bad bottle is a fluke
A manufacturing defect departs from the intended design.
Under the Restatement (Third) of Products Liability, a design defect claim generally requires:
A reasonable alternative design
The manufacturer’s intent
A departure from specifications
Privity with the manufacturer
The Third Restatement uses risk-utility with a reasonable alternative design.
MacPherson v. Buick Motor Co. held:
Manufacturers owe care to foreseeable users
Only the direct buyer can sue a manufacturer
Manufacturers are liable for every defect
Retailers are never liable
Cardozo dismantled the privity requirement for negligence claims.
A product has a foreseeable, non-obvious risk, and no warning is given. The best claim is:
Failure to warn
Manufacturing defect
No claim, if the design is sound
Express warranty only
Inadequate warnings are a separate defect category.
In Indiana Harbor Belt v. American Cyanamid, Judge Posner refused strict liability for shipping a toxic chemical by rail because:
Due care could prevent spills, so negligence sufficed
Chemicals like that are never dangerous
The railroad had consented to the risk of a spill
Strict liability covers only blasting
Strict liability is for risks that care cannot control.
Rylands v. Fletcher imposed strict liability for:
Escape of a dangerous thing from non-natural land use
All accidents happening on privately owned land
Negligent construction of reservoirs only
Injuries suffered by trespassers
A reservoir flooded a neighbor's mine shafts. Rylands is a root of abnormally dangerous activity liability.
A pedestrian is hit by a car whose brakes were defectively manufactured. Can she sue the manufacturer in strict products liability?
Yes: foreseeable bystanders can recover
No: only buyers can sue
No: she wasn’t using the product
Only in negligence
Courts extend strict products liability to foreseeable bystanders.
Spano v. Perini: blasting vibrations damaged a garage, with no debris landing on it. The court held:
Strict liability even without physical invasion
Liability required debris to land on the property
Negligence had to be proved
Blasting is common usage
Strict liability for blasting covers concussion damage too.
Justice Traynor's concurrence in Escola v. Coca-Cola argued for strict products liability mainly because:
Makers can best reduce hazards and spread costs
Consumers are too careless to protect themselves
Juries are unable to find negligence
Contract law already requires it
Traynor's loss-spreading and deterrence rationale was adopted in Greenman.
Soule v. General Motors held that the consumer expectations test:
Doesn’t fit complex technical design questions
Applies to every design defect claim, however complex
Replaces risk-utility in all cases
Applies only to food and drink products
Ordinary consumers lack expectations about complex designs, like crash performance.
Barker v. Lull Engineering: once the plaintiff shows the design proximately caused injury, under the risk-benefit test:
The defendant must prove benefits outweigh risks
The plaintiff must prove an alternative design
The case is dismissed
The jury must find negligence
Barker allows either consumer expectations or risk-benefit with a burden shift.
Under the learned intermediary doctrine, a prescription drug maker generally satisfies its duty to warn by warning:
The prescribing doctor
Every patient directly
The pharmacist only
The FDA only
Exceptions include mass vaccinations and, in some states, oral contraceptives (MacDonald v. Ortho).
Hood v. Ryobi: a man removed a saw's blade guards despite warnings and was injured. The court held the warnings:
Were adequate without listing every consequence
Were inadequate for not explaining results
Were irrelevant to misuse
Created strict liability
Too much detail can dilute warnings; clear, prominent warnings sufficed.
Riegel v. Medtronic held that state tort claims challenging a medical device approved through FDA premarket approval are:
Preempted
Never preempted
Allowed only for punitive damages
Allowed if filed in federal court
By contrast, Wyeth v. Levine held drug labeling claims generally are not preempted.
A product is used in a foreseeable but unintended way (standing on a chair). The manufacturer:
Must design against foreseeable misuse
Has no responsibility for misuse
Is strictly liable for all uses
Is protected by the learned intermediary rule
Only unforeseeable misuse defeats or reduces the claim.
A kitchen knife cuts a user who was careless. A failure-to-warn claim fails because:
There’s no duty to warn of obvious dangers
Knives are unavoidably unsafe
The user assumed every risk
Knives are services
Warnings are required for non-obvious risks.
Boomer v. Atlantic Cement: a cement plant's dust and vibration was a nuisance. The court:
Awarded permanent damages instead of shutting the plant down
Enjoined the plant immediately
Found no nuisance because the plant was so economically valuable
Awarded only nominal damages
The court balanced the plant's economic value against the harm.
Spur Industries v. Del E. Webb: a developer built homes near a cattle feedlot, then sued. The court:
Enjoined the feedlot but made the developer pay to move it
Denied relief because the developer came to the nuisance
Awarded punitive damages
Found the feedlot strictly liable
Coming to the nuisance shaped the remedy rather than barring relief.
Fontainebleau Hotel v. Forty-Five Twenty-Five: a new tower shaded a neighboring hotel's pool. The court held:
No nuisance: there’s no right to a neighbor’s light and air
A nuisance requiring the tower’s removal or redesign
A trespass on the hotel’s land
Strict liability for blocking sunlight
Florida law recognized no easement for light and air absent agreement.
Private nuisance protects mainly against:
Substantial, unreasonable interference with land use
Any physical entry onto the land by a person or thing
Harm shared by the general public
False statements about the property
Trespass protects exclusive possession; nuisance protects use and enjoyment.
A private person may sue for a public nuisance only if she:
Suffered harm different in kind from the public
Lives in the same city where the nuisance is located
Filed a criminal complaint about it
Owns property anywhere in the state
The special injury rule limits private suits for public nuisance.
At common law, owners of livestock that wander onto a neighbor's land and trample crops were:
Strictly liable
Liable only if negligent
Never liable
Liable only for punitive damages
Livestock trespass was a traditional strict liability category, modified in some fence-out states.
fill: Strict liability applies to abnormally ___ activities like blasting.
A product that departs from its intended design has a ___ defect.
Under the Restatement (Third), a design defect claim generally requires a reasonable ___ design.
A private nuisance is a substantial and unreasonable interference with the use and ___ of land.

topics.name: Defamation & Privacy
terms: Defamation
A false, defamatory statement of fact about the plaintiff communicated to a third party.
Libel
Defamation in written, printed or other fixed form.
Slander
Spoken, transient defamation.
Slander per se
Spoken defamation actionable without special damages, such as accusing someone of a crime.
Publication
Communicating a statement to someone other than the plaintiff.
Actual malice
Knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth.
Public figure
A person with pervasive fame, or who voluntarily entered a public controversy.
Special damages
Proven financial losses, such as a lost job or contract.
Of and concerning
The requirement that a statement reasonably be understood to refer to the plaintiff.
Substantial truth
A complete defense when the gist of the statement is accurate.
Absolute privilege
Complete immunity for statements in judicial, legislative and certain official proceedings.
Qualified privilege
Conditional protection for statements serving a shared interest, lost by abuse.
Opinion
A statement not provably false, protected unless it implies false facts.
Intrusion upon seclusion
An intentional, highly offensive invasion of another’s private affairs.
Public disclosure of private facts
Publicizing intimate matters that are highly offensive and not of legitimate concern.
False light
Publicity portraying someone inaccurately in a way highly offensive to a reasonable person.
Appropriation
Using another’s name or likeness for one’s own benefit without consent.
Right of publicity
The ability to control commercial use of one’s identity.
Republication
Repeating another’s defamatory statement, which can create liability for the repeater.
Fair report privilege
Protection for accurate accounts of official proceedings and government records.
Section 230
Federal statute shielding online platforms from liability as publishers of users’ content.
Single publication rule
Treats one edition of a book or newspaper as one publication for suit purposes.
Defamatory meaning
A tendency to harm reputation or deter others from associating with the plaintiff.
cases: New York Times v. Sullivan
Public officials must prove actual malice to recover for defamation.
Curtis Publishing v. Butts
The actual malice standard extends to public figures.
Gertz v. Robert Welch
Private figures need not prove actual malice, but states cannot impose liability without fault.
Dun & Bradstreet v. Greenmoss Builders
Presumed and punitive damages are allowed without actual malice on purely private matters.
Philadelphia Newspapers v. Hepps
A plaintiff suing over speech of public concern must prove falsity.
Milkovich v. Lorain Journal
There is no separate privilege for opinion; statements implying provable false facts are actionable.
Hustler Magazine v. Falwell
Public figures cannot recover for emotional distress from a parody without actual malice.
Snyder v. Phelps
Funeral protest speech on public issues was shielded from IIED liability.
Zeran v. America Online
An internet service was immune from liability for third-party postings.
Zacchini v. Scripps-Howard
Broadcasting a performer’s entire act violated his right of publicity.
Midler v. Ford Motor Co.
Imitating a famous singer’s distinctive voice in an ad was appropriation.
Shulman v. Group W Productions
Recording an accident victim in a rescue helicopter could be intrusion.
Nader v. General Motors
Wiretapping and overzealous surveillance could support an intrusion claim.
Time, Inc. v. Hill
False light claims about matters of public interest require actual malice.
mcq: New York Times v. Sullivan requires a public official suing for defamation about official conduct to prove:
Actual malice, by clear and convincing evidence
Mere negligence, proved by a preponderance of the evidence
Special damages and nothing more
Repetition of the statement to others
The First Amendment requires knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth.
In defamation law, 'actual malice' means:
Knowing falsity or reckless disregard of truth
Ill will or hatred toward the plaintiff personally
Intent to harm the plaintiff’s business
Any careless mistake about the facts
Despite its name, actual malice concerns the speaker's attitude toward truth, not spite.
A false, damaging post on a social media site is best classified as:
Libel
Slander
Neither, because it is online
Slander per se only
Written or fixed-form defamation is libel.
Which statement is NOT a traditional slander per se category?
Saying someone is rude at parties
Accusing someone of a serious crime
Saying someone has a loathsome disease
Attacking someone's competence in their trade
Slander per se categories don't require proof of special damages.
A columnist writes, 'In my view, the mayor's budget plan is idiotic.' Most likely:
Protected opinion
Libel per se
Slander
An actionable insult
Milkovich: there is no wholesale opinion privilege, but statements not provably false or implying false facts are protected.
Al writes a defamatory letter to Bo, seals it, and mails it. Only Bo reads it. Defamation?
No: no third party received it
Yes: writing it is enough
Yes: it is libel per se
Only if Bo is offended
Publication means communication to someone other than the plaintiff.
A newspaper reports that a man spent three days in jail; he actually spent two. His defamation claim likely:
Fails: the statement was substantially true
Succeeds: any false detail at all is actionable
Succeeds as libel per se
Fails only if he is a public figure
Substantial truth is a complete defense.
A newspaper accurately quotes a source who falsely accuses a teacher of theft. The newspaper:
Can be liable as a republisher
Is never liable for quoting others
Is liable only if it invented the quote
Is protected by Section 230
Republishing defamation can create liability, subject to privileges like fair report.
A website hosts a user's defamatory review. Under Section 230, the website is generally:
Immune from publisher liability for user content
